answer:
**HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, assumption-driven):** Among the 97 Psychology studies in the Reproducibility Project (RPP; `project=='rpp'`), **approximately 46% of successfully replicated studies — 16 of 35 (`replicated==1`; exact binomial 95% CI 28.8%–63.4%) — had a junior professor as the most senior author of the REPLICATION team**, where "junior professor" is defined as the seniority label `Assistant` or `Assistant Professor` (Researcher excluded). Under this reading, junior professors are in fact the largest seniority class among replication-team leaders of successfully replicated RPP studies: 16/35 (Assistant 6 + Assistant Professor 10), versus Professor 8/35, Associate Professor 7/35, Researcher 4/35.

This is one defensible reading, not "the" correct answer. The estimate swings under every other defensible interpretation:
- **Include Researcher in "junior"** → 57.1% (20/35; CI 39.4%–73.7%).
- **Seniority from original authors (`seniority.o`)** → 0% (0/35; CI 0%–10.0%), because the `seniority.o` column contains NO Assistant/Assistant Professor labels at all in the Psychology subset (only Professor 83, Associate Professor 9, Researcher 5 across all 97 rpp studies); including Researcher gives 2.9% (1/35).
- **Denominator = all 97 rpp studies instead of the 35 successful replications** (seniority.r, junior excl. Researcher) → 39.2% (38/97; CI 29.4%–49.6%).

**Full sensitivity table (all 8 combinations, exact Clopper–Pearson 95% CIs):**

| Denominator | Seniority source | Junior definition | n | k | Proportion (95% CI) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| replicated==1 (35) | seniority.r | Asst + Asst Prof | 35 | 16 | 45.7% (28.8–63.4) |
| replicated==1 (35) | seniority.r | Asst + Asst Prof + Researcher | 35 | 20 | 57.1% (39.4–73.7) |
| replicated==1 (35) | seniority.o | Asst + Asst Prof | 35 | 0 | 0.0% (0.0–10.0) |
| replicated==1 (35) | seniority.o | Asst + Asst Prof + Researcher | 35 | 1 | 2.9% (0.1–14.9) |
| all rpp (97) | seniority.r | Asst + Asst Prof | 97 | 38 | 39.2% (29.4–49.6) |
| all rpp (97) | seniority.r | Asst + Asst Prof + Researcher | 97 | 54 | 55.7% (45.2–65.8) |
| all rpp (97) | seniority.o | Asst + Asst Prof | 97 | 0 | 0.0% (0.0–3.7) |
| all rpp (97) | seniority.o | Asst + Asst Prof + Researcher | 97 | 5 | 5.2% (1.7–11.6) |

**What drives the differences / data-integrity confirmations:**
- The near-total driver of the discrepancy is the seniority source: `seniority.o` for the Psychology subset contains only {Professor, Associate Professor, Researcher} — zero Assistant/Assistant Professor labels — so any original-author reading yields ~0%. The `seniority.r` reading is the only one where junior-faculty ranks appear (and are actually the modal class among replication leaders of successful replications).
- The rpp subset is clean: 97 rows = 97 unique ids (0 duplicated ids, unlike ml1/ml3 which have multiple lab rows per study id), and `project`, `replicated`, `seniority.o`, `seniority.r`, `discipline` are all fully populated (0 missing). The 27 missing `replicated` values and all duplicated `id` rows lie outside Psychology, so the denominators 35 and 97 are exact and no imputation was required.
- Adopted interpretation (explicit): Psychology = `project=='rpp'`; "replicated studies" = `replicated==1` (p≤0.05, same direction); "junior professor" = {Assistant, Assistant Professor}; seniority = most senior author of the replication team (`seniority.r`). This yields the headline estimate ~46% (16/35).

**Workflow executed:** load CSV → verify schema/missingness → filter `project=='rpp'` (n=97) → split `replicated==1` (n=35) vs all 97 → crosstab seniority.o / seniority.r × replicated → compute counts and exact binomial 95% CIs for all 8 reading combinations → confirm no missing/duplicates affect the Psychology subset.

payload.hypothesis: Approximately 46% (16/35; 95% CI 29-63%) of successfully replicated Psychology (RPP) studies had a junior professor (Assistant or Assistant Professor) as the most senior author of the replication team; junior professors were the largest seniority class among replication-team leaders of successfully replicated RPP studies.
